details: Ukraine nuclear fleet: 15 operating VVER reactors at 4 sites; total capacity ~13.8 GWe; provides ~55-60% of Ukraine's electricity (2019 baseline); under normal conditions; 2022-2025 war disrupted generation significantly; Westinghouse fuel supply from 2022 fully replacing Russian TVEL fuel; all are VVER-1000 design (PWR analog; negative void coefficient)
safety_or_significance: 15 operating VVER = none can have RBMK-type prompt criticality; negative void coefficient → self-limiting physics; containment buildings at all sites; fundamentally safer than Chernobyl RBMK design; war creates external threats to safety systems not inherent reactor physics vulnerabilities
source: IAEA PRIS database 2025; Energoatom annual reports; WNA Ukraine 2025; SNRIU

details: Khmelnytsky NPP (KhNPP): Unit 1 first power 1987; Unit 2 first power 2004; 2 × VVER-1000 (950 MWe net each); total 1900 MWe capacity; remotely located in NW Ukraine away from main conflict zones; Units 3 and 4 under construction (partially completed in Soviet era; restart of construction approved; VVER-1000 design); ~50 km from Polish border
safety_or_significance: KhNPP far from Russian-controlled territory 2022-2025; no direct occupation threat; however part of national grid under attack; Units 3-4 construction represents major expansion of Ukrainian nuclear capacity to reduce dependence on Russian gas; European investment (EBRD) being sought
source: IAEA PRIS; WNA Ukraine; Energoatom KhNPP; SNRIU

details: Rivne NPP (RNPP): 4 units operating; Units 1-2: VVER-440/V-213 (420 MWe net each); Units 3-4: VVER-1000 (950 MWe net each); total 2740 MWe; first power Unit 1 = 1980; Unit 4 first power = 2004; oldest Ukrainian nuclear station; VVER-440 reactors slightly different design from VVER-1000 but still negative void coefficient; western Ukraine; remotely located
safety_or_significance: VVER-440 (Units 1-2) vs VVER-1000 (Units 3-4): VVER-440 has smaller reactor vessel; multiple steam generators; slightly different safety systems; both designs have negative void coefficient; VVER-440 does not have full containment building (only protective shell) — minor design difference from VVER-1000; no fuel incidents 2022-2025
source: IAEA PRIS; WNA Ukraine; NEA/CRPPH/R(2024)3; Energoatom

details: South Ukraine NPP (SUNPP): 3 × VVER-1000 (950 MWe net each); total 2850 MWe; Unit 1 first power 1982; Unit 3 first power 1989; southern Ukraine near Mykolaiv; not under occupation; Yuzhnoukrainsk ~200 km from front line 2022-2024; NPP on Southern Bug River; Unit 4 construction began but stopped
safety_or_significance: South Ukraine NPP on Southern Bug River = cooling water supply; unlike ZNPP (Kakhovka Reservoir) this plant not in immediate war zone threat as of 2025; however Russian missile/drone strikes have hit Ukrainian energy infrastructure broadly; national grid instability causes forced load-following which stresses VVER reactors (designed for baseload)
source: IAEA PRIS; Energoatom SUNPP; SNRIU annual report 2023

details: ZNPP under Russian occupation: see zaporizhzhia_npp_2022_2025_REAL.csv; largest capacity 6000 MWe; before 2022 ZNPP provided ~20% of Ukraine electricity alone; occupation removes these 6 units from Ukrainian grid = approximately 1/3 of Ukraine's pre-war nuclear capacity; Russian forces have operated site with non-Ukrainian staff from 2023
safety_or_significance: Loss of ZNPP capacity forced Ukraine to: (1) reduce electricity exports; (2) increase thermal generation (gas/coal); (3) accelerate other NPP fuel switch to Westinghouse; ZNPP in cold shutdown since Sep 2022 = 0 MWe generation; war's single largest energy impact on Ukraine
source: zaporizhzhia_npp_2022_2025_REAL.csv; Energoatom; NEA report 2024; IEA Ukraine 2022

details: Ukraine completed transition from Russian TVEL nuclear fuel to Westinghouse AP1000 fuel assemblies for VVER-1000 reactors: partial switch began 2015 (South Ukraine NPP); accelerated 2022 after Russian invasion; full transition completed by 2023 for VVER-1000 units; Westinghouse VVER fuel manufactured in Sweden (Västerås); also UK (Springfields); compatibility engineering required adapting Westinghouse fuel geometry to Soviet reactor design
safety_or_significance: Pre-2022: Russia (TVEL/Rosatom) supplied 100% of Ukrainian reactor fuel; post-2022: complete independence from Russian fuel supply; political/energy security imperative; technical challenge: VVER-1000 fuel designed by Russians → Westinghouse required requalification; first Westinghouse fuel cycles showed some fuel rod vibration issues (remedied by 2019 design changes); now routine
source: Westinghouse press release 2022-2023; SNRIU; Energoatom; WNA Ukraine; NEA 2024

details: Installed nuclear capacity Ukraine: 15 reactors total 13,800 MWe; available without ZNPP (6×1000=6000 MWe occupied): 7,800 MWe from 9 operating units at 3 sites; actual available capacity 2022-2025 further reduced by Russian missile strikes on switchgear/transformer stations forcing emergency shutdowns; lowest available: ~4000 MWe winter 2022-23
safety_or_significance: Ukraine 2021 (pre-war): 85 TWh nuclear generation = 55% of total electricity; 2022: grid attacks caused rolling blackouts; nuclear capacity factor fell; nuclear still provided ~50% of available generation; October-November 2023 strikes specifically targeted NPP switchyard transformers (not reactors; same threat as ZNPP external power supply vulnerability)
source: IAEA PRIS; IEA 2022; Ukrainian Energy Ministry; NEA/CRPPH/R(2024)3

details: SNRIU (Derzhatomrehulyuvannya): Ukrainian nuclear safety regulator; established post-independence; IAEA member; WANO member; oversees licensing of all nuclear facilities; during 2022-2025 war: SNRIU jurisdiction over ZNPP technically maintained (under international law) but physically inaccessible; SNRIU continued oversight of 3 unoccupied NPP sites
safety_or_significance: SNRIU working with IAEA to maintain regulatory standards at non-occupied plants despite wartime conditions; loss of ZNPP to Russian control = regulatory gap that IAEA monitoring partially fills; SNRIU publishes annual safety reports; SNRIU-IAEA cooperation agreement for post-war NPP return assessment
source: SNRIU annual reports; IAEA SNRIU partnership; WNA Ukraine

details: Ukraine nuclear electricity share: 55-60% pre-war (highest fraction in Europe after France); 85 TWh/year from nuclear (2019); total generation ~160 TWh/year; nuclear = baseload; renewables: 7%; hydro: 7%; gas/coal: remainder; this high nuclear fraction was deliberate policy for energy independence from Russian gas
safety_or_significance: High nuclear fraction = Ukraine extremely exposed when ZNPP occupied (lost ~25% total national generation) AND grid attacks hit remaining nuclear infrastructure; shows strategic value of nuclear to Ukraine and why ZNPP occupation was not just a safety issue but an energy warfare tool
source: IEA Ukraine 2022; Energoatom annual report 2021; IAEA PRIS; WNA Ukraine 2025

details: Energoatom (National Nuclear Energy Generating Company of Ukraine): state-owned enterprise operating all 4 NPP sites; 4 sites × capacity 13,800 MWe total; 35,000+ employees pre-war; responsible for: fuel procurement; operations; maintenance; decommissioning; Chernobyl site management; transformed to company structure 1996 from Ministry of Energy
safety_or_significance: Energoatom headquarters Kyiv; continued operations 2022-2025 from non-occupied sites; worked with IAEA and Westinghouse to maintain fuel supply; ZNPP Energoatom operators remained on-site under Russian occupation through 2022-2023 (under coercion); some relocated to Energoatom-run facilities in other cities
source: Energoatom corporate; WNA Ukraine; IAEA DG reports

details: Russian strikes on Ukrainian nuclear infrastructure: specifically targeted not reactor buildings but: (1) 750 kV switchyards (external power supply) at all NPPs; (2) transmission lines; (3) backup transformers; deliberate strategy to create station blackout risk without attacking reactor containment directly; at least 6 incidents of emergency shutdown at non-occupied NPPs due to external power loss 2022-2024
safety_or_significance: IAEA recorded 9 separate incidents at Ukrainian nuclear sites (non-ZNPP) 2022-2024 related to external power supply threats; each triggers emergency diesel generator activation; same fundamental risk as ZNPP; at non-occupied sites: Ukrainian staff maintained cooling; restored external power within hours to days; no loss of cooling events reached safety threshold
source: IAEA Ukraine situation reports 2022-2024; NEA 2024; IAEA Director General quarterly reports

details: Budapest Memorandum on Security Assurances Dec 5 1994: Ukraine surrendered Soviet nuclear weapons (1900 strategic + ~2500 tactical = third largest nuclear arsenal globally) in exchange for: (1) respect for sovereignty and existing borders; (2) refusal to threaten or use force; (3) economic coercion ban; signatories: US, UK, Russia; also signed: Ukraine; Belarus and Kazakhstan signed similar; weapons transferred to Russia by 1996
safety_or_significance: Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2014 and 2022 = direct violation of Budapest Memorandum; Ukraine's nuclear disarmament in 1990s was largest voluntary nuclear disarmament in history; context for why ZNPP occupation is internationally contested; demonstrates failure of non-proliferation framework when guarantor state becomes aggressor; relevant to future NPT regime
source: Budapest Memorandum Dec 5 1994 official text; Wilson Center; Arms Control Association; post_soviet_ukraine_nuclear_context_REAL.csv

details: Ukrainian nuclear waste management: ISF-1 (interim spent fuel storage at Chernobyl): 2001-2022; 1261 RBMK fuel assemblies stored; ceased accepting new assemblies 2022 (war/security); ISF-2 (Holtec International facility at Chernobyl): opened 2020; capacity 21,217 fuel assemblies from all 4 NPP sites; VVER fuel: 1698 assemblies stored by Jan 2022; ZNPP spent fuel: stored on-site in dry casks (see zaporizhzhia_npp_2022_2025_REAL.csv)
safety_or_significance: ISF-2 construction was politically contested: initial US DOE design (2000) replaced by Holtec International contract; delayed 20 years by legal disputes; opened 2020 just before invasion; ZNPP dry cask storage (on-site) not accessible to Energoatom during occupation; Ukraine has no permanent deep geological repository (planned for 2050s); spent fuel currently interim storage only
source: chernobyl_unit_operations_REAL.csv; Energoatom; Holtec; NEA 2024; IAEA ZNPP updates

details: WANO (World Association of Nuclear Operators): established 1989 directly in response to Chernobyl accident; Ukraine/Energoatom full member; peer reviews at Ukrainian NPPs; Moscow Center serves former Soviet sites (however Russia-Ukraine member interactions suspended 2022); peer reviews document safety culture improvements; WANO training programs for Ukrainian operators
safety_or_significance: WANO was created because INSAG-7 (1992) identified poor nuclear safety culture as root cause of Chernobyl (alongside reactor design flaws); Ukraine's WANO membership and IAEA partnerships = post-Soviet nuclear safety culture transformation; however human factors remain primary uncertainty (as at all NPPs globally)

details: Ukraine nuclear fleet post-war outlook: Energoatom target: all 15 reactors continue operation through 60-year license extension (to ~2035-2064 depending on unit); new build: KhNPP Units 3-4 (VVER-1000; partially built); feasibility study for SMR (Small Modular Reactor) technology (NuScale/Westinghouse); ZNPP return to Ukrainian control prerequisite to resuming generation; EU nuclear support for energy independence
safety_or_significance: Energy independence from Russia = primary driver for maximizing nuclear capacity; Ukraine post-war will likely be largest nuclear generator in Europe by capacity; fuel supply security through Westinghouse partnership; decommissioning of old VVER-440 at Rivne (Units 1-2) likely long-term; new VVER design (VVER-TOI) with enhanced passive safety considered
source: Energoatom strategy 2035; WNA Ukraine 2025; EU REPowerEU; Westinghouse Eastern Europe strategy
